'''David Kelly Campbell''' (born July 23, 1944) is an American [[theoretical physicist]] and academic administrator. His research has included [[high-energy physics]], [[Condensed matter physics|condensed-matter physics]], [[nonlinear dynamics]], and [[chaos theory]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=Topics in Nonlinear Science: Dedicated to David K. Campbell’s 80th Birthday |url=https://pubs.aip.org/collection/13400/Topics-in-Nonlinear-Science-Dedicated-to-David-K |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=AIP Publishing |language=en}}</ref> He has held academic and research positions at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]], [[the Institute for Advanced Study]], [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], and [[Boston University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. David K. Campbell |url=https://people.bu.edu/dkcampbe/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=people.bu.edu}}</ref> He served as director of the Center for Nonlinear Studies at Los Alamos National Laboratory, head of the Department of Physics at the [[University of Illinois]], dean of the College of Engineering at [[Boston University]], and provost of Boston University.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Skandalakis |first=Irene |title=Physics professor David K. Campbell wins distinguished SigmaPhi Prize |url=https://dailyfreepress.com/11/13/22/200647/physics-professor-david-k-campbell-wins-distinguished-sigmaphi-prize/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=The Daily Free Press}}</ref> He is a [[fellow of the American Physical Society]] and a co-recipient of the [[American Physical Society]]'s 2010 [[Lilienfeld Prize|Julius Edgar Lilienfeld Prize]]. <ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Prize Recipient |url=http://havlin.biu.ac.il/HTMLfiles/lilienfeldprize.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304104158/http://havlin.biu.ac.il/HTMLfiles/lilienfeldprize.html |archive-date=2016-03-04 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=havlin.biu.ac.il |language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Campbell was born on July 23, 1944, in [[Long Beach, California]]. He attended [[Harvard College]], where he received a Bachelor of Arts degree in chemistry and physics, ''summa cum laude'', in 1966.<ref name=":6" /> He subsequently studied mathematics at the [[University of Cambridge]], completing Part III of the Mathematics Tripos with distinction in 1967. He received a Ph.D. in theoretical physics and applied mathematics from Cambridge in 1970.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. David Campbell |url=https://www.jmu.edu/news/cohencenter/2015/10-02-campbell.shtml |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=www.jmu.edu |language=en}}</ref>

As an undergraduate at Harvard, Campbell was elected to the Senior Sixteen of Phi Beta Kappa and shared the Sophia Freund Prize.<ref name=":7" /> In 1966, he was awarded a [[Marshall Scholarship]] to study at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]].

== Career ==
After completing his doctorate, Campbell joined the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]], where he worked as an instructor and research associate in physics and as a fellow in the Center for Advanced Study from 1970 to 1972. From 1972 to 1974, he was a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]]. The Institute's records list his membership in its School of Natural Sciences from September 1972 to June 1974.<ref name=":1" />

In 1974, Campbell joined [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory]] as a J. Robert Oppenheimer Fellow. He subsequently became a staff member of Los Alamos National Laboratory, where he worked from 1977 to 1992. From 1985 to 1992, he served as director of the laboratory's Center for Nonlinear Studies. He also held an adjunct professorship at the University of New Mexico from 1990 to 1992.<ref name=":8" />

Campbell returned to the University of Illinois in 1992 as professor of physics and head of the Department of Physics. He remained department head until 2000.<ref name=":4" />

In 2000, Campbell joined [[Boston University]] as a professor of physics and electrical and computer engineering. He served as dean of the College of Engineering from 2000 to 2005. He was provost ad interim from 2004 to 2005 and served as provost from 2005 to 2011. He subsequently continued his research and teaching at Boston University as a professor of physics, electrical and computer engineering, and materials science and engineering.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Ecke |first=Robert E. |date=2024-04-19 |title=The center for nonlinear studies: A personal history |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0204698 |journal=Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=042102 |doi=10.1063/5.0204698 |issn=1054-1500|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Editorial work ===
Campbell's editorial career has been closely associated with nonlinear science. He was the founding editor-in-chief of ''[[Chaos (journal)|Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science]]'', serving from the journal's establishment in 1990 through 2016.<ref name=":4" />

In 2015, he published "The pre-history of ''Chaos''—An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science," describing the events and scientific activities that preceded the establishment of the journal.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last=Campbell |first=David K. |date=2015-08-19 |title=Editorial: The pre-history of Chaos—An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4928745 |journal=Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science |volume=25 |issue=9 |pages=090401 |doi=10.1063/1.4928745 |issn=1054-1500}}</ref>

== Research ==
Campbell's research has covered several areas of [[theoretical physics]]. His early work included high-energy and nuclear physics<ref>{{Cite web |title=Academy of Europe: CV |url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Campbell_David/CV |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=www.ae-info.org}}</ref>, while much of his later research has focused on [[nonlinear dynamics]], [[condensed-matter physics]], correlated electronic systems, and [[complex systems]]. His work has addressed solitons, polarons, nonlinear excitations, conducting polymers, superconducting materials, [[Semiconductor|semiconductor systems]], [[graphene]], and the dynamics of [[nonlinear systems]].<ref name=":10" />

=== Solitons and conducting polymers ===
During the 1980s, Campbell conducted theoretical research on nonlinear excitations in quasi-one-dimensional materials, particularly conducting polymers such as polyacetylene. His work examined solitons and polarons arising from interactions between electrons and lattice distortions.<ref name=":11" />

In work with collaborators including Alan Bishop, he studied soliton excitations in [[polyacetylene]] and their relationship to relativistic field-theory models.<ref name=":12" /> Other research examined polarons in quasi-one-dimensional conducting polymers and their structure and optical properties.<ref name=":11" />

Campbell also investigated soliton energetics in Peierls-Hubbard models and nonlinear excitations in condensed-matter systems.<ref name=":13" /> His later research extended these interests to intrinsic localized modes and nonlinear excitations in solids and Bose–Einstein condensates.<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last=Campbell |first=David K. |last2=Flach |first2=Sergej |last3=Kivshar |first3=Yuri S. |date=2004-01-01 |title=Localizing Energy Through Nonlinearity and Discreteness |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/localizing-energy-through-nonlinearity-and-discreteness |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=43–49 |doi=10.1063/1.1650069 |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Nonlinear dynamics and chaos ===
Campbell became involved in nonlinear science and chaos research during his years at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]]. His work included nonlinear waves, kink and antikink interactions<ref name=":16" />, discrete nonlinear systems<ref name=":15" />, and chaotic dynamics. He was also involved in the development of the interdisciplinary community surrounding nonlinear science.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":8" />

Campbell was the founding editor-in-chief of ''Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science''. He served in that position from 1990 to 2016.<ref name=":14" />

His research has also included the [[Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou problem|Fermi–Pasta–Ulam problem]], concerning the dynamics of nonlinear coupled oscillators. In 2005, Campbell coauthored a review of the first 50 years of research on the problem.<ref name=":17" /> His subsequent work has examined the Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou recurrence problem and metastable states in related nonlinear systems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pace |first=Salvatore D. |last2=Reiss |first2=Kevin A. |last3=Campbell |first3=David K. |date=2019-11-06 |title=The β Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou recurrence problem |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5122972 |journal=Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science |volume=29 |issue=11 |pages=113107 |doi=10.1063/1.5122972 |issn=1054-1500|arxiv=1908.00564 }}</ref>

Campbell's later research has also addressed correlated electronic systems, functional renormalization-group methods, [[graphene]] and other two-dimensional materials, and intrinsic localized modes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Renormalization group approach to graphene bilayers |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2512.23349v1 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=arxiv.org |language=en}}</ref> 

== Awards and honors ==
Campbell received several academic distinctions while at [[Harvard College]]. He was elected to the Senior Sixteen of [[Phi Beta Kappa]]<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=David Campbell named Phi Beta Kappa Visiting Scholar {{!}} Boston University Physics |url=http://physics.bu.edu/internal/news_items/show/271 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=physics.bu.edu}}</ref> and shared the Sophia Freund Prize.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2010-04-15 |title=Who won the Sophia Freund prize in 2009 and before 1997? |url=https://talk.collegeconfidential.com/t/who-won-the-sophia-freund-prize-in-2009-and-before-1997/880116 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=College Confidential Forums |language=en}}</ref> In 1966, he received a [[Marshall Scholarship]] to study at Cambridge.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |date=2017-04-06 |title=David Campbell |url=https://theconversation.com/profiles/david-campbell-357696 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Campbell was selected as a [[National Academy of Sciences]] Exchange Scientist to the Soviet Union in 1977.<ref>{{Cite web |title=David K. Campbell {{!}} Santa Fe Institute |url=https://www.santafe.edu//people/profile/david-k-campbell |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=www.santafe.edu |language=en}}</ref> His later international academic appointments included visiting professor at the [[University of Dijon]] in France in 1984 and 1985, Emil Warburg Lecturer at the [[University of Bayreuth]] in Germany in 1990, Toshiba Lecturer at [[Keio University]] in Japan in 1994, Deutsche Bank Distinguished Lecturer at the [[University of Frankfurt]] in 1994, C. N. Yang Visiting Professor at the [[Chinese University of Hong Kong]] in 1996<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=David Campbell {{!}} Physics |url=https://www.bu.edu/physics/profile/david-campbell/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=www.bu.edu |language=en}}</ref>, and Stanislaw M. Ulam Scholar at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] in 1998–1999.<ref name=":1" />

Campbell was elected a [[Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1988 and a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1990.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=David Campbell, PhD {{!}} College of Engineering |url=https://www.bu.edu/eng/profile/david-campbell/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=www.bu.edu}}</ref>

He later served as Gauss Professor at the [[Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities]] in Germany in 2014–2015<ref>{{Cite web |title=David Campbell receives Gauss Professorship {{!}} Boston University Physics |url=http://physics.bu.edu/internal/news_items/show/254 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=physics.bu.edu}}</ref>, and as a visiting scholar at the [[International Institute of Physics]] at the [[Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte]] in Natal, Brazil, from 2014 to 2016. He was also a Phi Beta Kappa Visiting Scholar from 2015 to 2016.<ref name=":3" />

In 2010, Campbell received the [[Lilienfeld Prize|Julius Edgar Lilienfeld Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]], jointly with physicist [[Shlomo Havlin]]. <ref name=":2" />The prize recognized their contributions to physics and their communication of the significance of physics to broader audiences. 

In 2020, Campbell was named a co-recipient of the Sigma Phi Prize in Statistical Physics. The prize is awarded every three years to three statistical physicists for outstanding achievements in the field. The 2020 award was presented at the 2023 SigmaPhi conference in Greece because of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. Campbell was recognized for work concerning the mechanisms by which microscopically reversible, non-integrable dynamical systems approach statistical equilibrium or remain in nonequilibrium metastable states.<ref name=":1" />

In 2025, ''Chaos'' published a focus issue marking Campbell's 80th birthday and highlighting research areas associated with his career, including nonlinear science, chaos, localized states, and condensed-matter systems. <ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Introduction to Focus Issue: Topics in Nonlinear Science |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2508.01801v1 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=arxiv.org |language=en}}</ref>
